title: Perf Regression Canary (Prod) — Overview
author: Noah Patel
body:
## Summary
The **Perf Regression Canary** is a low-footprint production workload that continuously exercises representative LLM inference requests (prefill+decode, streaming and non-streaming) across a curated set of **models, regions, and critical runtime configuration slices**.

It is designed to detect **p95 latency** and **tokens/sec** regressions early—before they impact broad customer traffic—and to page the right oncall with enough context to triage quickly (runtime build, kernel selection, scheduler mode, GPU type, batch composition).

This page is the high-level overview (problem statement, why we need a prod canary, ownership, and current coverage). See the design doc for the full architecture and the metrics spec for exact definitions.

---

## Problem statement
We have strong pre-merge and pre-release benchmark coverage, but we still see performance regressions escape into production due to:

- **Fleet heterogeneity** (multiple GPU SKUs and driver/runtime variants across regions)
- **Production-only contention** and noisy neighbors (node-level interference, background maintenance)
- **Scheduler/batching interactions under mixed traffic** that are hard to reproduce in a lab
- **Kernel autotune drift** and dynamic kernel selection differences at production sequence lengths
- **Streaming-specific pitfalls** (TTFT alignment, chunking overhead, first-token timestamp bugs)

When a regression makes it to customers, it often shows up as:

- elevated **tail latency** (p95/p99) on a single model or region
- a drop in sustained **decode throughput** (tokens/sec)
- instability over time (variance spikes) that is difficult to attribute quickly

We need an always-on, production-adjacent signal that is:

- **small and safe** (does not impact customer SLOs)
- **slice-aware** (model/region/GPU/runtime build/scheduler mode)
- **actionable** (pages with direct links + debugging context)

---

## Why a production canary (vs offline benchmarks)
Offline benchmarks remain required for gating changes, but they are not sufficient.

### Offline benchmarks are good at
- catching obvious throughput/latency regressions in controlled conditions
- validating algorithmic changes (kernel-level improvements, quantization settings)
- reproducible A/B comparisons on fixed hardware

### Offline benchmarks miss
- **live scheduler dynamics** (continuous batching heuristics + queue composition)
- **real deployment rollouts** (regional rollouts, mixed fleet, partial canaries)
- **observability pipeline correctness** (aggregation windows, label propagation)
- **production runtime toggles** (feature flags, runtime config pinning, kernel fallback paths)

### The canary complements the lab
The canary is intentionally narrow: it is not a full representation of customer workloads. It is a regression detector for **serving runtime health in production**.

---

## Goals (v1)
1. **Continuous signal**: Stable time-series for per-slice p95 latency and tokens/sec.
2. **Fast detection**: Alert on regressions above thresholds versus a baseline (see ADR).
3. **High-quality paging**: Avoid false positives through warmup handling, minimum sample size, and deploy-window suppression.
4. **Actionable context**: Every alert includes enough metadata to quickly narrow attribution (runtime build, git SHA, kernel id, scheduler mode, GPU SKU, batch stats).
5. **Low operational risk**: Canary traffic is rate-limited and uses a canary-safe request class so it cannot starve or contend with customer queues.

## Non-goals (v1)
- Customer-facing “perf SLA” or external perf dashboarding.
- Replacing the benchmark lab or pre-release performance gating.
- Exhaustive workload coverage (we explicitly constrain model list and prompt shapes).

---

## What we measure (high level)
For each canary slice, we collect and alert on:

- **Latency**
  - End-to-end request latency (p95)
  - Streaming: time-to-first-token (TTFT) p95 and end-to-end p95 (where supported)
- **Throughput**
  - Tokens/sec (decode) with consistent start-time semantics (streaming and non-streaming)
- **Stability / noise indicators** (used for debugging and to explain variance)
  - batch composition (prefill/decode counts)
  - max/avg sequence length observed
  - queue depth / scheduler wait time (where available)
  - KV cache hit/eviction indicators (if enabled for the model)

Exact definitions, windows, and label schema are documented in: `architecture-and-standards/observability-standards/perf-canary-metric-spec`.

---

## How regressions are detected (baseline strategy)
We alert on regressions vs a baseline, with suppression during known noisy periods.

Current strategy (see ADR-0231):
- Primary baseline: **rolling baseline** (e.g., last 7d median for the same slice)
- Optional comparison: **pinned “known-good” runtime build** baseline (used during rollout phases and for high-risk releases)
- Guardrails:
  - minimum sample size per window
  - warmup exclusion after canary start / runtime deploy
  - deploy-window suppression (to avoid paging during active rollout propagation)

---

## Ownership and oncall routing
### Primary owners
- **Serving Runtime (Kernel + Scheduling)**: instrumentation, runtime version tagging, interpreting regressions
  - Exec sponsor: Mateo Alvarez
  - Perf architecture: Noah Patel
  - Scheduling: Sofia Ivanova
  - Kernel performance: Hiro Tanaka
  - Instrumentation: Omar El-Sayed
- **SRE/Infra**: alert policy, paging hygiene, incident integration
  - Lead: Sean Gallagher
  - Integration: Rafael Mendes
  - Runbook/paging hygiene: Tomáš Novák
- **Telemetry/Observability**: metrics definitions, aggregation/cardinality controls, dashboards
  - Lead: Logan Wright
  - Metric definitions: Nadia Rahman
  - Ingestion: Caleb Johnson
  - Cardinality controls: Thomas Baird

### Alert flow (v1)
1. Canary detector fires -> **pages SRE oncall** (initial signal quality + impact assessment).
2. If confirmed to be real (not a pipeline or noise artifact) -> **assign/engage Runtime** (kernel/scheduler attribution).
3. If correlated with a runtime deploy -> follow rollback procedure in the runbook.

See: `eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets/perf-regression-alert-policy` and `eng-sre/runbooks/runbook-perf-canary-regression-triage`.

---

## Current status and coverage
### Status
- Project phase: **Phase 1 rollout** (limited region + limited models)
- Canary traffic class: **canary-safe** (strict rate limits + priority controls)
- Dashboards: available (internal), with deploy annotations enabled
- Alerting: enabled for Phase 1 slices; thresholds tuned conservatively to avoid paging storms

### Coverage matrix (as of 2026-02-21)
Notes:
- Model list is intentionally small in Phase 1 to validate stability/noise and label propagation.
- GPU SKUs are explicitly sliced to avoid blending heterogeneous performance.

| Region | GPU SKU | Models (canary) | Modes | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| us-east-1 | H100-80GB | llama-3.1-8b-instruct | streaming + non-streaming | Primary Phase 1 slice; scheduler pinning enabled |
| us-east-1 | H100-80GB | mistral-7b-instruct-v0.3 | streaming + non-streaming | Used to validate TTFT + tokens/sec semantics |
| us-east-1 | A100-80GB | llama-3.1-8b-instruct | non-streaming | Secondary slice for fleet heterogeneity sanity checks |
| eu-west-1 | (planned) | (planned) | (planned) | Phase 2 expansion after alert tuning + overhead verification |

### What is NOT covered yet
- Broader model catalog (larger parameter counts and long-context variants)
- APAC regions
- Full matrix of scheduler modes (experimental heuristics are pinned off in Phase 1)
- Model-specific baselines (Phase 1 uses generic thresholds; we will move to per-model expectations)

---

## What to do when you get paged
If you are paged for a perf regression:

1. Open the alert payload and confirm:
   - model + region + gpu_sku + runtime_build
   - which metric regressed (p95 latency, TTFT p95, tokens/sec)
   - baseline type (rolling vs pinned known-good)
2. Validate signal quality:
   - check sample size and variance panels
   - confirm deploy annotation alignment (recent runtime change?)
3. Compare slices:
   - same model across GPU SKU
   - same slice across region (if available)
   - same slice across runtime_build (if canary sees mixed builds during rollout)
4. Follow the runbook for mitigation/rollback and trace capture.

Primary reference: `eng-sre/runbooks/runbook-perf-canary-regression-triage`.
